title: Data Centers in Orbit: Google Prepares AI Satellite Launch
summary: Google prepares to launch artificial intelligence satellites into orbit for data center connectivity
detailed: Moving computing systems beyond Earth is gradually becoming part of the long-term plans for major tech companies.
Google intends to test how effectively artificial intelligence can operate not in conventional ground-based data centers, but directly in orbit.
If successful, Google will be positioned to advance orbital computing and evaluate the feasibility of utilizing space-based infrastructure to support AI services.
Google has partnered with Blue Origin to launch satellites equipped with AI servers into low Earth orbit.
sentences: Moving computing systems beyond Earth is gradually becoming part of the long-term plans for major tech companies.
Google intends to test how effectively artificial intelligence can operate not in conventional ground-based data centers, but directly in orbit.
To realize this vision, the company has enlisted Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s aerospace venture.
The partners aim to create a network of satellites capable of executing computing tasks using specialized Google processors.
The collaboration between Google and Blue Origin involves launching computing hardware aboard the heavy-lift New Glenn rocket.
The mission is scheduled for the first quarter of 2029.
The satellites are planned to be placed in a sun-synchronous orbit, a trajectory that allows for relatively constant lighting conditions while orbiting the Earth.
Each unit will be powered by Google’s proprietary Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), designed specifically for AI workloads.
It is expected that a cluster of orbital computing nodes will provide performance comparable to a standard server rack in a traditional data center.
In other words, this is not merely about satellites for data collection or transmission, but about building hardware capable of autonomous processing in space.
The project builds upon the Project Suncatcher initiative.
Looking ahead, Google aims to develop an orbital computing network that would allow for running AI models and processing massive datasets outside of terrestrial infrastructure.
Thus, the company is exploring an alternative approach to resource deployment.
Before scaling up the project, Google conducted a preliminary proof-of-concept test.
In October, the company sent an experimental satellite equipped with its specialized AI processor into orbit.
Trials confirmed that the onboard TPU chip is capable of performing computing operations directly in space.
One of the test tasks involved running the Gemma 4 language model.
It generated a short haiku, which was then transmitted back to Earth.
Despite the small scale of the experiment, it successfully validated several key elements: the operation of computing hardware in orbit, model deployment, and data transmission.
However, the first mission differed significantly from the upcoming launch.
The experimental unit was sent as a secondary payload on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, sharing the flight with other satellites.
The next phase will be organized differently: Google plans to utilize the New Glenn for a dedicated launch specifically focused on the objectives of Project Suncatcher.
The current strategy marks a departure from the traditional model where all primary computing is concentrated in land-based data centers.
Project Suncatcher is intended to verify whether a distributed infrastructure can be created where satellites not only provide connectivity but also perform complex computational tasks autonomously.
The 2029 launch will serve as a critical milestone in transitioning from a single experimental unit to a larger-scale system.
If successful, Google will be positioned to advance orbital computing and evaluate the feasibility of utilizing space-based infrastructure to support AI services.
